record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: How can unfairness be measured and corrected in federated settings where sensitive group membership is unavailable, including making approaches such as distributionally robust optimization and multicalibration scale to the large, high-dimensional regime typical of federated learning and developing new theory for fairness without explicit sensitive attributes?

evidence.quote: Both measuring and correcting unfairness in contexts where there is no data regarding sensitive group membership is a key area for federated learning researchers to address. ... The challenge of how to make these approaches work for large-scale, high-dimensional data typical to federated settings is also an open problem ... Finally, the development of additional theoretical approaches to deﬁning fairness without respect to “sensitive attributes” is a critical area for further research.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning setting in which a global model is trained collaboratively across a large number of clients, each holding private local data, without sharing raw data with a central server or with other clients. Suppose that for every data point, the value of any "sensitive" attribute (such as race, gender, age, or other protected group membership) is unavailable to all parties — neither clients nor the server may observe or store such attributes. The trained global (or personalized) model is then deployed to make predictions on data drawn from the union of client distributions.

Formalize and resolve the following three intertwined questions in this setting:

1. (Measurement) Define a quantitative notion of "unfairness" of a predictor f : X → Y that (a) does not require access to sensitive group labels at training or audit time, (b) is well-defined when data are partitioned across many clients with heterogeneous, non-IID local distributions, and (c) reduces to a meaningful classical group-fairness criterion (e.g., demographic parity, equalized odds, or calibration across groups) when sensitive attributes happen to be observable. Provide an estimator of this quantity that can be computed under the communication and privacy constraints of federated learning, together with finite-sample guarantees.

2. (Correction / algorithms) Design federated training algorithms that provably reduce the unfairness measure from (1). In particular, develop scalable federated counterparts of distributionally robust optimization (DRO) — i.e., algorithms that minimize the worst-case loss over an appropriately chosen ambiguity set of subpopulations — and of multicalibration — i.e., algorithms that guarantee calibration of f simultaneously over a rich family C of subsets of X — such that the per-round communication, per-client computation, and total sample complexity scale at most polylogarithmically (or otherwise tractably) in the dimension d of the feature space, the number of clients n, and the complexity (e.g., VC dimension) of C. Prove convergence and fairness guarantees for these algorithms under standard federated assumptions (partial participation, client heterogeneity, local SGD updates, and differential privacy).

3. (Theory of fairness without sensitive attributes) Develop a theoretical framework for defining and reasoning about fairness when sensitive attributes are not available even in principle. Specifically, identify axiomatic conditions a notion of "fairness without sensitive attributes" should satisfy, characterize the family of all such notions, prove impossibility or possibility theorems analogous to those known for classical group fairness, and clarify the relationship between such attribute-free notions and DRO-, multicalibration-, and individual-fairness-based formulations.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent works (2023–2025) propose partial approaches — distributionally robust federated algorithms (e.g., DRDM, unbalanced-Wasserstein DRO), provable group-fairness calibration frameworks like FedFACT, proxy-sensitive-attribute methods, and LLM-based fair recommendation without sensitive attributes — but the broader problem of scalable, theoretically grounded measurement and correction of unfairness in high-dimensional federated settings without any sensitive-attribute information, including federated multicalibration with provable guarantees and a unifying theory of attribute-free fairness, remains an active and largely open research direction.

status_evidence.title: FedFACT: A Provable Framework for Controllable Group-Fairness Calibration in Federated Learning
status_evidence.snippet: Provable framework for controllable group-fairness calibration in federated learning, addressing fairness in FL but still relying on group information.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress on provable group-fairness calibration in FL; does not resolve attribute-free case.

status_evidence.title: Distributionally Robust Federated Learning with Client Drift Minimization
status_evidence.snippet: DRDM combines DRO with dynamic regularization, framing training as a min-max problem to maximize worst-case client performance.
status_evidence.claim: Recent DRO-based federated algorithms exist but scalability and attribute-free fairness theory are not fully addressed.

status_evidence.title: Fairness in Federated Learning: Trends, Challenges, and Opportunities (2025 survey)
status_evidence.snippet: Survey identifies open challenges including fairness without sensitive attributes and scaling multicalibration-style guarantees in federated regimes.
status_evidence.claim: Survey lists this as an ongoing open challenge as of 2025.
